blocks.md: This lesson follows **Forward State Propagation and Occlusion Decay** in *Spatial Memory* (Vol IV).

blocks.source: Vol IV, Spatial Memory, § Forward State Propagation and Occlusion Decay
blocks.md: When a sensor loses sight of a moving body, bringing the machine to a safe stop takes time and demands a usable state estimate throughout the deceleration interval. Forward propagation bridges this blind duration by projecting the most recent observation forward in time, whether the machine continues an authorized task or executes a protective fallback. A learned generative model can predict future trajectories autoregressively, and ensemble dispersion or Monte Carlo rollouts can quantify prediction variance. However, statistical spread alone does not constitute a certified upper bound on physical tracking error.

questions.q: The section **Forward State Propagation and Occlusion Decay** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: A belief stops supporting motion when its validated error bound, growing from the evidence epoch, first reaches the task tolerance, and free space erodes inward from the unobserved boundary at a hidden agent's speed bound.
Every spatial claim carries evidence, estimate, and publication epochs, and only a physical measurement advances the evidence epoch, so prediction and republishing must preserve it.

A state estimator alternates a prediction that widens uncertainty with elapsed time and updates that narrow it below every input by inverse-variance fusion, applying each measurement at its capture epoch and replaying out-of-sequence ones.
Space last seen free stays free only until an unseen agent could have entered it, so occluded free space shrinks at that agent's speed bound and blind crossings need site controls, not memory.
